summary:
Our group went through several significant changes and discussions that slowed our
progress, but these experiences ultimately helped us better understand, strengthen, and improve both our challenge and our proposed solution. Here are the changes we made:
1. Adjustments to the project’s approach, specifically regarding the programming method and game design.
2. Internal conflicts among team members—stemming from disagreements over
roles—forced us to restructure the entire project.
3. The original concept proved unfeasible, requiring us to pivot and plan something
different.

How We Approached the Challenge

We began by entering the planning and preparation phase. This was followed by extensive research into every element to be included in our game—from the materials (including their weight and value) to the mechanics of real-world space missions, which we studied through various examples. We then moved on to the programming and development phase. This proved to be very challenging; while some team members focused on this, others worked on the presentation to ensure we stayed on track.
details:
Our project is called MISSION CONTROL. It is an educational simulator designed to help people understand how rockets work and what it takes to complete a space mission. In the game, players can learn about the different parts of a rocket, what each component does, and how all the pieces work together.

Players can build their own rockets by adding different components, such as engines, fuel tanks, structural parts, communication systems, and other equipment. Each component has its own characteristics and affects the mission in different ways, including the rocket's weight, fuel consumption, available power, and overall budget.

Once the rocket is ready, players can launch it and watch a simulation of the mission. Things do not always go as planned, and that is part of the learning experience. If the rocket fails to launch properly, does not reach the required altitude, or has problems during the mission, the simulator explains what happened and why. Players can then make changes to their design and try again. If the mission is successful, the game also provides a report with the results.

The simulator also helps players understand that planning a space mission involves more than just building a rocket. They need to think about the mission's goal, the technology required, the amount of fuel, the total weight, the available resources, and the orbit they want to reach. Every decision can affect the final result.

Tools and Resources

To develop this project, we used Godot Engine 4.7.2 as our game engine, GDScript to program the simulator's features and logic, and Visual Studio Code as a supporting tool for working with the code.

We also explored educational and technical resources related to space exploration and mission design. These included NASA's CubeSat 101 guide, information about Concept Maturity Levels (CML), and tools such as GMAT and NASA Mission Viz. We used these resources as references to learn more about space missions, mission planning, and how space systems are designed and analyzed.

What We Hope to Achieve

We hope MISSION CONTROL makes learning about space exploration more fun, interactive, and accessible. We want children, students, and anyone interested in science and technology to be able to experiment, build their own rockets, make decisions, and discover some of the challenges involved in a real space mission.

Our main goal is to make learning more practical. Instead of only reading about rockets, players can test their ideas, make mistakes, understand what went wrong, and try again. Every attempt is an opportunity to learn something new about engineering, rocket launches, and space exploration.
